opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is not in building a slightly better wrapper around a model. Every time the base model improves, a lot of that work gets absorbed. If your whole value is "we prompt GPT or Claude a bit better," that advantage disappears in six months.

What I find more interesting is the environment and the context the agent operates in. A model by itself is like a very smart person who just walked into your company. They're capable, but they don't know your codebase, your customers, your internal tools, or the unwritten rules of how things get done. So much of the value of a human employee comes from accumulated context and from being plugged into the right workflows. For agents it's the same. Startups that own a specific environment, with its tools, data, feedback loops and the memory of what happened before, have something that doesn't automatically get commoditized when the next model comes out.

Second, I think a lot about what I'd call the "second half" of AI. In the first half we focused on methods and models, and we measured progress on benchmarks. Now the methods are general enough that the bottleneck shifts to defining the right problems and the right evaluations. What does it actually mean for an agent to be useful in this job? How do you measure it? How do you get reward signals from real usage? A startup that deeply understands one domain and can define what "good" looks like there, and then collect that signal, has a real moat, because that's exactly what the general model companies don't have.

Third, interaction design. Right now most agents are used either like a chatbot, where you ask and it answers, or a fully autonomous thing you send off and hope it comes back right. There's a big space in between: how humans and agents collaborate over long horizons, how the agent asks for help, how trust gets built so you can delegate more over time. I don't think anyone has figured out the right product form yet. In the past, new capability often created new interfaces, like the browser or the smartphone. I suspect agents will need their own.

So if I were advising a founder, I'd say don't bet against the model getting better. Assume it will be much better, and ask: what becomes possible then that's still hard for the model company to do? Usually the answer is something about owning the context, the environment, the user relationship and the feedback data in a specific place. That's where I'd look.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the opportunity is shifting, and a lot of people are still building for the world of two years ago.

When models were weaker, the value of an agent startup was in the scaffolding. You wrote the prompts, you built the tool wrappers, you handled retries and memory and all the glue, and that glue was most of the product. I was part of that era, with ReAct and the early agent work, and I think it was genuinely useful. But that layer is being absorbed. Every time a new model comes out, a chunk of what startups built as "agent infrastructure" just becomes a model capability. If your moat is that you taught the model to call tools in a loop, you don't have a moat.

So where's the opportunity now? I'd put it in two places.

The first is environments and evaluation. The thing that's actually scarce isn't intelligence anymore, it's a well-defined task with a real feedback signal. If you can build the environment where an agent operates in a specific domain, with the right tools, the right state, and most importantly a way to tell whether it did the job well, you're building something the model labs can't easily replicate, because it requires domain knowledge and real users and real consequences. SWE-bench is a small example of this. The companies that own the environment for legal work, or for accounting, or for lab science, will have something durable, and the model becomes a component that keeps getting better for free.

The second is the long-horizon, high-stakes work where reliability matters more than raw capability. Models are very good at a single clever step. They're still uneven at running something for days, recovering from mistakes, knowing when to stop and ask. That gap is where product work matters, and it's not going away as fast as people assume, because the way you close it is partly with better models but partly with system design, with how you structure the task, how you expose state, how you let a human intervene.

What I'd avoid is anything that's essentially a thin layer on a general capability. Horizontal "AI assistant for X" products that just wrap the model will get squeezed from both sides. And I'd be skeptical of frameworks as businesses. Frameworks are great for research and for teaching, but the half-life is short.

The other thing I'd say, which is maybe less of a startup answer, is that the most interesting opportunities right now might be in domains where nobody has even written down what the task is. A lot of real work doesn't have a benchmark because nobody thought of it as a problem you could formalize. The founders who go in and do that formalization, who turn messy knowledge work into something with a clear environment and reward, are doing something close to research, and I think that's where the real leverage is.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is in closing the gap between what a model can do and what a customer can actually use. A more capable model doesn’t automatically become a reliable product. You still need to understand the workflow, connect the right tools and data, and figure out when the agent should act versus ask a person for help.

So I would look for a specific area where you can own the whole feedback loop. You deploy the agent, observe where it fails, and have a clear way to measure whether it’s getting better. That gives you something valuable beyond access to the same model everyone else has: an understanding of the task and the experience of making it work in practice.

The question I’d ask is: if the model becomes ten times better, does your product become much more useful, or does the reason for your product disappear? You want to build something where better models let you solve more of the customer’s problem. Start with a narrow task, make it work, and expand as the capabilities improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to take responsibility for a complete task. As models become more capable, more of the underlying intelligence becomes available to everyone. But there’s still a lot of work between having a capable model and having a system that reliably does something useful for a customer.

For example, a customer doesn’t really want an agent that can use a browser. They want a particular business process completed correctly. To deliver that, you need to understand the workflow, connect to the right systems, handle exceptions, and know when to ask a human for help. You also need a way to measure whether the task actually succeeded.

So I would look for a specific area where you can get close to users and build that whole loop. Ideally, every improvement in the underlying model makes your product more useful and lets you take on more of the work. The question is: as intelligence gets better and cheaper, what can you now deliver that people will pay for?
